entry.summary: Day 4 | Tesla’s next big distraction will be announcing a SpaceX/Tesla merger. Tell me I'm wrong. The company is officially trapped in a game of corporate one upmanship with its...
entry.content: Day 4 | Tesla’s next big distraction will be announcing a SpaceX/Tesla merger. Tell me I'm wrong. The company is officially trapped in a game of corporate one upmanship with itself. Every single time they hit an operational wall, they pull a shiny new object out of the hat to completely reset the valuation clock. Just look at the receipts: • 2017: The Roadster is promised for 2020 to distract from Model 3 “production hell.” • 2019: With the Roadster nowhere near ready, the Cybertruck is suddenly unveiled. • 2021: Cybertruck faces massive delays? Enter a guy dancing in a spandex suit as the “Tesla Bot.” • 2024: The $25k mass-market car gets quietly shelved, and hours later, the Cybercab hype machine drops. • 2026: Facing flat deliveries and major earnings pressure, Tesla stages an over-the-top, totally unbuyable “flying” Roadster stunt at a SpaceX facility—while quietly pushing production back to 2028. Seriously, once you’ve weaponized rocket thrusters on a sports car to make people forget about a 9yr production delay, where else can you possibly go? You merge for now. The massive integration of SpaceX engineers and facilities for that recent Roadster air show wasn’t just a cool stunt. It was a strategic narrative pilot. By teasing a merger, Musk can completely decouple Tesla’s stock from the automotive growth plateau it’s currently facing. It throws the ultimate narrative shield over the brand, forcing Wall Street to treat it like a trillion dollar business on the level of Nvidia and Apple. All while completely burying the reality that the Roadster still won't be ready in 2028 when he announces the merger late next year. And no, this is not the end. There's still an endless horizon of AI networks and planetary humanoid labor fleets to pivot to when the run into there next inevitable production delay. But right now, a SpaceX merger is big enough for their next distraction in 2027. This is no disrespect to Elon Musk, the man is the best there ever was at this in my opinion. He understands human psychology and market mechanics better than any CEO in history. The real shame here belongs to us. As consumers, investors, and media outlets, we willingly let him off the hook every single time. We get so intoxicated every time he promises the next sci-fi shiny object that we completely forget about the trail of broken promises left in the rearview mirror. Are we ever going to hold him accountable, or are we all just waiting in line to buy whatever he hypes next? Let me know your thoughts! #Tesla #SpaceX #CorporateStrategy #MandA #Valuation #Leadership #Marketing

entry.title: Tell Me I'm Wrong | Day 3: Zooming Doesn't Make It Bigger
entry.summary: Tell Me I'm Wrong | Day 3: Zooming Doesn't Make It Bigger. Didn't get the results you expected from that expensive marketing campaign you spearheaded? Don't panic. Just zoom in!...
entry.content: Tell Me I'm Wrong | Day 3: Zooming Doesn't Make It Bigger. Didn't get the results you expected from that expensive marketing campaign you spearheaded? Don't panic. Just zoom in! Six months ago, awareness was sitting comfortably at 55%, and you confidently told the execs, "Given how targeted this campaign is, we feel a 10pt increase to 65% in product awareness is more than achievable!" They approved your budget and 6 months later, the campaign is over, and awareness only went up to 59%. Well, shit... The executive meeting is in a few days, and you're staring at Excel wondering how you're going to explain spending half the company's annual marketing budget to deliver less than half the improvement you projected. Don't worry! I'll show you how to get out of that meeting with your head still attached! First, let's just hope nobody remembers that 10pt commitment from six months ago. Next, throw those results on a simple bar graph. "But Joe, this looks terrible!" Hold on, I haven't finished yet! Right now it's not exactly the visual you're hoping to put in front of execs, and I know that. So go to the chart settings, start that Y axis at 52% and cap it at 60%. BOOM! Your 7.3% relative increase in awareness now looks more than TWICE as tall as before the campaign! Same numbers. Same results. Completely different visual story. Now get your story straight and say "Our strategic marketing initiative generated significant positive momentum in top-of-funnel awareness, validating our targeted go-to-market approach and strengthening the foundation for customer acquisition!" Beautiful! Your missed target now sounds like a strategic victory! Don't pause though! Move quickly to the next slide, highlight some positive customer feedback, and wrap things up before anyone starts asking uncomfortable questions. Oh, this is very important! Make sure you request that all questions be held until the end. And just like that, I've saved your presentation! You're welcome. All sarcasm aside, I've spent enough time in corporate meetings to wonder whether people genuinely don't notice how data is presented or simply prefer the story they're being told. When you're more concerned with making your results LOOK successful than understanding why you missed your target, you lose out on everything that data could actually teach you. That's the data worth looking into before spending another dollar. Instead, everyone's admiring a pretty graph. That's the power of data visualization, and exactly why we need to be careful with it. You may not know you are being misled and honestly, many people don't realize they're being misleading. Excel can automatically truncate the Y-axis. So, tell me I'm wrong. I believe graphs showing percentages should almost always start at 0 and end at 100. Your audience shouldn't have to recalibrate their eyes every time someone changes the Y-axis. If you need to zoom in to make a change visible, maybe you're using the wrong graph.

entry.summary: Tell Me I'm Wrong | Day 1: The easiest way to lie with data is to tell the truth. You don't have to make up numbers to mislead people. Sometimes all you have to do is leave out ...
entry.content: Tell Me I'm Wrong | Day 1: The easiest way to lie with data is to tell the truth. You don't have to make up numbers to mislead people. Sometimes all you have to do is leave out the ones that don't support your argument. I've spent over a decade in market research, and few things frustrate me more than watching good research get twisted to justify decisions someone already made. Now imagine a company testing a new product. Research shows that 88% of respondents would consider buying it, but only 17% say they're "very likely" to purchase it at the proposed price. Guess which number makes it into the executive presentation? "88% OF CUSTOMERS WOULD CONSIDER BUYING OUR NEW PRODUCT!" Technically true! Sounds like a winner! Never mind that only 17% expressed strong purchase intent at that price, or that production costs might force the price even higher. The research did its job. The presentation didn't. And lets not pretend this only happens in business. We all cherry-pick information to support our arguments, conveniently leaving out details that don’t “work” for us. Looking at data isnt the same as understanding what it actually tells you. An accurate statistic can still support a completely misleading narrative. So, tell me Im wrong. At what point does selectively presenting the truth become lying?

entry.content: My beautiful daughter is nearing 9 months old and becoming a parent has been one of the most profound periods of personal growth in my life. It has changed how I think about time, responsibility, ambition, and the kind of future I want to build. The past few years have brought a lot of transition and challenges, but becoming a father has given me a clearer sense of direction. It has made me more intentional about the work I pursue, the people I learn from, and the kind of impact I want to have. That clarity has also changed how I think about my career. I still care deeply about doing thoughtful, useful work. I still enjoy solving messy problems, understanding people, and helping teams make better decisions through research, customer insight, and strategy. But now, the reason behind that work feels sharper. I want to build stability. I want to contribute to work that matters. I want to keep growing into the kind of professional, partner, and father my daughter can look up to. This next chapter feels less about proving myself and more about building something meaningful.

entry.summary: Market research doesn’t always reveal the truth about your customers’ virtues Let’s be honest. No one wants to look dumb in front of their peers. We nod along when someone bring...
entry.content: Market research doesn’t always reveal the truth about your customers’ virtues Let’s be honest. No one wants to look dumb in front of their peers. We nod along when someone brings up a topic we don’t understand. We laugh at jokes we don’t get because everyone else is laughing. We say “of course” when we’re unsure — because it’s easier than admitting we’re lost. This happens in market research too. People take surveys with the best intentions, but they still shape their answers to look smart, responsible, or virtuous. They say a message was clear when it wasn’t. They say they support sustainable products, even if they rarely buy them. They say they bought an EV to save the planet — but it was really to save money. I’ve spent years running research in the EV space, including conjoint studies to understand what actually drives adoption and financials consistently rises to the top. Lower fuel costs. Lower maintenance. Federal and state incentives. Time-of-use charging savings. HOV lane access. Environmental values are good for storytelling. But financial value is what changes behavior. This gap between stated values and actual behavior shows up everywhere — not just in EVs. And it’s measurable. A meta-analysis of 28 stated preference studies found that people overstate their willingness to pay by a median factor of 1.35 (Little & Berrens, 2004). When market research gives people space to protect their self-image, it’s no longer revealing behavior. It’s capturing aspiration. If you’re building strategy based on stated intent, without validating it through behavioral data or tradeoff modeling, you’re not grounded. This is where research becomes strategy. And this is what I help companies do — connect what people say with what they actually do. If you’re working through that gap, let’s connect.

entry.content: So much market research is badly designed, and no one realizes it until it’s too late Too many companies trust that their market research is solid because they hired a vendor to run it. But I’ve seen too many surveys that look fine on the surface and are garbage underneath. Poorly framed questions Biased answer options No logic checks No exclusivity No internal consistency It happens at utilities, government agencies, nonprofits, startups. Everywhere. And the worst part is no one realizes it until they’ve already made decisions that affect budgets, operations, or public trust. Here’s a small but personal example. When I lived in Sacramento, I got a survey from the local parks department. They were planning $50,000 in updates to two neighborhood parks I used almost daily. I wanted to give feedback. The survey was a disaster. They used government park names that no one locally used. You could say you didn’t own a dog and then later say you brought your dog to the park every day. They let you select multiple activities and still choose “none of the above.” No one who reviewed that survey thought through what the data would look like. And I knew they’d just roll it up, report the totals, and build a plan around bad inputs. That money was going to be wasted and this kind of thing happens more than people realize. It is not about whether you used Qualtrics or had a pretty dashboard. If the research design is broken, your insights are worthless. Collecting bad data is worse than collecting no data. It leads to confidence in the wrong direction. This is why it matters who designs your research. Good survey design takes experience, curiosity, and the ability to spot problems before they become outcomes. I work with teams to get this part right because everything that follows depends on it. If this resonates with you or your team is navigating a similar challenge, feel free to connect. I am always open to trading stories and helping where I can.
